title: Indra Surrenders and Begs Forgiveness
story:
When the storm had passed and the hill stood whole again, the lord of heaven found that he could not stay away. For seven days he had poured his fury over Vrindavan — thunder and wind and water without mercy — because the cowherds, at a boy's urging, had turned their worship away from him. He had meant to teach them what it cost to forget their king. Instead the rain had broken against a mountain held up on the palm of a child, and Indra had been left holding nothing but the ruins of his own pride.

So he came down quietly, and he came alone. He approached in seclusion, ashamed, his offense heavy on him, for by now he had seen and heard enough of Krishna's boundless power to know exactly who stood before him. There was no thunder now, no elephant, no retinue. The forest around them had gone quiet after the rain, the leaves still wet and the ground soft underfoot, and there was no witness to what followed. The king of the gods walked into that stillness like a man come to settle a debt.

And he did the one thing a king does not do. He touched Krishna's feet with his crown.

The crown was the whole of his sovereignty, and he laid it at the feet of a cowherd boy who had not yet left his childhood behind. Then he spoke, and the words were not the words of a god addressing a child, but of a man undone.

"I was drunk on my own lordship," he said. "I did not know your power, and so I offended you. Forgive me, Lord. Let such a wish never rise in me again."

He did not stop at apology. The pride that had sent the storm, he confessed, had blinded him — for a man intoxicated with rule and riches cannot see the hand that holds the rod of punishment. He had looked at Krishna and seen only a boy. Now, in that quiet place, he named what he saw instead: the father and teacher of all the worlds, the lord before whom everything that breathes must bow, time itself with its punishment held ready. And he understood, too, why such a one had come down to walk among mortals at all — to lighten the burden of the earth, a burden the gods had carried long and could not lay down.

"By me," he admitted, "this home of the cowherds was nearly destroyed by wind and rain. And by you I have been spared. My arrogance is broken. My effort has come to nothing."

There was no long reproach. Krishna had never needed one. He had not struck Indra down; the rain had done that work for him, falling against the hill until the storm exhausted itself against a child's lifted hand. What Krishna gave now was not punishment but the thing that follows it.

"Go, Shakra," he said — Shakra being the name by which the gods had always known the lord of heaven. "May all be well with you. Do what I ask of you."

That was all. The pride that had darkened the sky did not need to be ground down any further. It had already let go of Indra the way a fist lets go of a stone. What remained was a king restored to his own dignity, sent back to heaven with a blessing where a wound might have been.
reflection: The surrender is complete before a single word of punishment falls, and that is the point. Krishna does not humble Indra; Indra's own pride breaks against what he has seen, and forgiveness arrives as a return — the moment the fist opens, the kingship is given back.
next_story_tease: But the surrender was not the end of it; Indra would soon return, not to beg, but to crown the boy Govinda with Surabhi the divine cow at his side.
hero_scene: Indra, king of the gods, kneeling in the quiet forest and touching his bright crown to the feet of the boy Krishna, his face lowered in shame as the last of the storm fades from the sky.
visual_elements: Indra bowing with crown at Krishna's feet
